title: Egg, yolk only, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: The egg yolk is the yellow part of the egg that contains almost all of the nutrients, including fats, vitamins, and minerals. When cooked without added fat (e.g., boiled or steamed), it retains most of its nutritional value.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The yolk holds nearly all the fat‑soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K.
Almost all of the egg’s biologically active iron is in the yolk.
Cholesterol content is high, but current research shows moderate intake does not raise blood cholesterol for most people.
Yolk acts as a natural emulsifier in sauces, mayonnaise, and custards.
Cooking preserves most of the yolk’s antioxidant compounds.

items.title: Rich in vitamins A, D, E, and K
items.content: These vitamins support vision, immune function, bone health, and blood clotting.

items.title: High‑quality protein source
items.content: Although less than the egg white, yolk protein contains all essential amino acids.

items.title: Contains lecithin
items.content: Lecithin aids brain function and promotes liver health.

items.title: Abundant choline
items.content: Choline is vital for memory, nerve signaling, and fat metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Carotenoids such as lutein and zeaxanthin protect the eyes from age‑related degeneration.

items.title: High cholesterol content
items.content: People with familial hypercholesterolemia should limit yolk consumption.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to yolk proteins.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked yolk can harbor Salmonella; cook until fully set.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked yolk without added fat can be eaten on its own, added to salads, sauces, purees, or used in baking as an emulsifier.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked yolks in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in small portions.
